scenes.tts: Around 1970, Martin Rodbell's laboratory studied how glucagon switches on adenylyl cyclase in liver membranes. In plain buffer, the hormone stuck to the membranes and would not wash off. Add A T P, and it came off within seconds. That was odd, since A T P is the enzyme's fuel.
scenes.caption: Around 1970, Martin Rodbell's laboratory studied how glucagon switches on adenylyl cyclase in liver membranes. In plain buffer, the hormone stuck to the membranes and would not wash off. Add ATP, and it came off within seconds. That was odd, since ATP is the enzyme's fuel.
scenes.visual: Liver membrane bar with glucagon stuck on; wash arrow leaves it in place; ATP chip added and glucagon floats off.
scenes.narration: Around 1970, Martin Rodbell's laboratory studied how glucagon switches on adenylyl cyclase in liver membranes. In plain buffer, the hormone stuck to the membranes and would not wash off. Add ATP, and it came off within seconds. That was odd, since ATP is the enzyme's fuel.

scenes.tts: The cause was a contaminant: commercial A T P carries a little G T P. Added on purpose, G T P proved to be required. Without it, glucagon barely switched the cyclase on. G T P was not the fuel. A trace was enough, so G T P was used over and over.
scenes.caption: The cause was a contaminant: commercial ATP carries a little GTP. Added on purpose, GTP proved to be required. Without it, glucagon barely switched the cyclase on. GTP was not the fuel. A trace was enough, so GTP was used over and over.
scenes.visual: ATP bottle with a GTP speck; two cyclase panels, without and with GTP; GTP fuel struck out; a single GTP chip loops while cyclic AMP chips accumulate.
scenes.narration: The cause was a contaminant: commercial ATP carries a little GTP. Added on purpose, GTP proved to be required. Without it, glucagon barely switched the cyclase on. GTP was not the fuel. A trace was enough, so GTP was used over and over.

scenes.tts: For years almost no other laboratory could reproduce this, because most were not working with membranes as clean as Rodbell's. Suppose the A T P is one percent G T P. Then the tube with no G T P added already holds enough for a full response, so the difference between tubes never appears. Many receptors switch on the same enzyme, and Rodbell thought it impossible that all were built into it. So he proposed a separate component between them, a transducer.

scenes.tts: The answer came from Alfred Gilman's laboratory at the University of Virginia. Gilman and Elliott Ross used cyc minus lymphoma cells, where the link between receptor and enzyme is missing. They added an extract from normal cells. The response came back, even when the extract's own cyclase was inactivated. So the transducer was a separate, movable protein.
